title: The Words That Ask, and the Word That Points Back
label: ch:ru-question-family
canDo: I can ask who, which and how many, hang a whole clause onto a noun with kotoryy, and both ask and embed a yes-or-no question with li.

payoff.summary: The question family the book opened at poka closes here at seven members, all one ancient stem: kto, chto, kakoy, kak, kogda, pochemu, skolko. Two of them supply their own answers by swapping the question-stem for the pointing-stem. kotoryy is the eighth relative of the same root and the one that does the most work -- it is how a Russian noun gets described at any length. li ends the chapter by turning out to have been inside ili since the joining chapter.
payoff.note: A second segment on SPINE-EXCHANGE-NAMES, the pre-A1 node whose QUESTION-WHAT the chto chapter realized. The relative kotoryy uses a track-local concept rather than the canonical RELATIVE-CLAUSE, which the ladder stages at B2 -- claiming that concept would move the track's reach without moving what a reader can do.
